note: The per-path comparison: what a megawatt from each supply path in config.PATHS costs, how long it takes to energise, and how available it is. Nobody publishes these eleven paths on one consistent basis, so this file is an assembly of separately published figures and the `caveat` on each row is what keeps the column from reading as a like-for-like comparison it is not. Rules for adding a row. (1) `path` is a key of config.PATHS and `metric` is a short noun phrase reused verbatim across paths ('levelised cost of energy', 'time to energisation', 'capacity factor'), because the page pivots on it; a metric spelled two ways becomes two rows that never meet. (2) `value` and `unit` are exactly as published — no unit conversion, no rounding, no averaging of two publishers, no midpoint of a range. A published range is two rows, a low and a high, each with its own caveat. (3) `year_dollars` is the cost basis the publisher stated. A cost with no stated dollar year cannot be compared with one that has it; write 'unstated' rather than assuming the publication year. (4) `vendor_claim` is true when the publisher sells the thing being measured. A fuel-cell maker's comparison of fuel cells against grid gas is evidence of what that vendor says, not of what is true, and the page labels it that way rather than dropping it — the vendors are often the only ones publishing at all. An independent lab, a regulator, a national laboratory or an ISO study is false. (5) `quote` is the short verbatim sentence the figure came from. (6) `caveat` states the basis: what is included (interconnection, fuel, land, emissions compliance), what is excluded, what region and what year, and whether the figure is a quote for one project or a class estimate. Every row needs one; a bare dollars-per-MWh across paths built on different scopes is the single most misleading thing this page could print. (7) `last_checked` is the day somebody last confirmed the row against `source_url`; after config.REFERENCE_STALE_DAYS days the page greys it. Cost curves move — a greyed row here is a prompt to look for a newer edition of the same study rather than to delete the old one. Working notes go in `curator_notes`, which pipelines/power/reference.py strips before anything can publish it; any other field containing a marker from WORKING_NOTE_MARKERS in that module is rejected outright.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The capital costs provided are overnight capital costs in 2023 price levels
rows.caveat: An engineering estimate in 2023 dollars for a generic 1,227 MW two-on-one H-class combined-cycle plant, including owner's costs and electrical interconnection but excluding interest during construction. It is not a price anybody was quoted: turbine prices rose steeply after 2023, so it is not comparable with the market-based capital costs in the two rows below.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 5 (CC 2x2x1, 2 x 1 H Class, 1,227 MW net).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Capital Cost $/kW $1,450 - $2,100
rows.caveat: The bottom of Lazard's 2026 range for a new gas combined-cycle plant, in dollars of a year Lazard does not state, so it cannot be put beside EIA's 2023-dollar estimate. Lazard says separately it has seen quotes of $2,400-$2,600/kW for projects completing after 2028, above its own range.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 assumptions page, Gas Combined Cycle column, low case (1,425 MW).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Capital Cost $/kW $1,450 - $2,100
rows.caveat: The top of Lazard's 2026 range for a new gas combined-cycle plant, for a smaller 725 MW configuration, in dollars of a year Lazard does not state. It is a financing-market number rather than an engineering estimate and is not comparable with EIA's 2023-dollar figure.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 assumptions page, Gas Combined Cycle column, high case (725 MW).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: Lazard's low case assumes the plant runs at a 90% capacity factor on $3.45/MMBtu gas, financed 60/40 at 8% debt and 12% equity. It is unsubsidised, carries no capacity payment and no carbon price, and assumes the plant exists: none of the interconnection or turbine-queue delay is priced in.
rows.curator_notes: Components at the low end: $25 capital, $1 fixed O&M, $3 variable O&M, $22 fuel.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: Lazard's high case is the same technology run at a 30% capacity factor, which is why the capital component per MWh is nearly four times the low case. A capacity factor assumption, not a cost difference, drives most of the spread, so neither end should be read as the cost of a plant dedicated to a data center.
rows.curator_notes: Components at the high end: $92 capital, $10 fixed O&M, $5 variable O&M, $23 fuel.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Construction Time Months 24
rows.caveat: Construction time only. It begins when the plant starts being built, and excludes the gas turbine order queue, permitting and the interconnection study process - which are what actually set the date a data center gets power today.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 assumptions page, Gas Combined Cycle.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.A (capacity factors, fossil-fuel generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for the entire US combined-cycle fleet selling into wholesale markets, which is an economic outcome rather than a technical ceiling. A plant built to serve one data center would be expected to run much harder, so this is not the availability of a dedicated unit. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Natural Gas / Combined Cycle column.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: Net Plant Heat Rate, Higher Heating Value (HHV) Basis
rows.caveat: A design figure for a new two-on-one H-class plant on a higher-heating-value basis. It is a new-and-clean full-load number, so it is better than what the plant would average over a year with starts, part-load running and degradation, and it is not comparable with a vendor's lower-heating-value specification.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 5.

rows.source_name: GE Vernova, 7HA Heavy Duty Gas Turbine factsheet
rows.quote: A 7HA COMBINED CYCLE PLANT, NOW CAPABLE OF >64% EFFICIENCY
rows.caveat: A turbine maker's specification for a single 7HA.03 in one-on-one combined cycle at ISO conditions, on a lower-heating-value basis. Lower-heating-value figures are roughly a tenth better than the higher-heating-value basis EIA and Lazard use, so this cannot be placed beside them; the factsheet itself says its information is indicative and not warranted.
rows.curator_notes: Factsheet document code GEA35768 (05/2025); publish_date taken from the PDF creation date because the sheet gives only a month.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The capital costs provided are overnight capital costs in 2023 price levels
rows.caveat: Covers 150 MWac of single-axis-tracking solar plus a 50 MW / 200 MWh AC-coupled battery, expressed per kW of solar capacity, in 2023 dollars. A hybrid's cost per kW depends entirely on how much storage is bolted on, so it is not comparable with a standalone solar or standalone battery cost.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 17 (AC-coupled). The DC-coupled variant, Case 18, is $2,561/kW.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: Unsubsidised low case for 100 MW of utility solar paired with a 50 MW four-hour battery, assuming a 30% solar capacity factor and $40/MWh to charge the battery. It excludes the federal investment tax credit, so it is not comparable with the contracted renewable PPA prices under path C2, which are net of that credit.
rows.curator_notes: With the ITC, Lazard's range becomes $43-$135/MWh.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: Unsubsidised high case for the same solar-plus-storage configuration at a 20% solar capacity factor and higher battery cost. It is a new-build cost of energy, not a delivered firm-power cost: the pairing still does not supply a data center around the clock.
rows.curator_notes: Storage capital cost assumption $270-$365/kWh including inverter.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Construction Time Months 12
rows.caveat: Construction time only, for the generation and storage plant itself. It excludes land, permitting and the interconnection queue, which for grid-connected solar is by far the longer part of the wait.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 assumptions page, Solar PV + Storage - Utility.

rows.source_name: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up: 2026 Edition (slides)
rows.quote: The median project built in 2025 took 61 months
rows.caveat: Median months from interconnection request to commercial operation for projects of every technology that came online in 2025, pooled across six ISOs and 19 non-ISO balancing areas. It is not solar-specific, and it counts only projects that finished: of the capacity that entered queues from 2000 to 2020, just 13% had reached operation by the end of 2025.
rows.curator_notes: Slide 51. Median by size: 54 months for 100-200 MW, 59 months for 200 MW and above.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.B (capacity factors, non-fossil generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for the whole US utility-scale solar photovoltaic fleet, which is a resource limit, not a dispatch choice. It is measured against summer capacity and says nothing about when in the day the output arrives, which is the part that matters for a constant data-center load. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Solar / Photovoltaic column.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The estimate is presented as an overnight cost in 2023 dollars
rows.caveat: A 2023-dollar engineering estimate for two AP1000 units on a brownfield site, excluding interest during construction. Vogtle units 3 and 4, the only AP1000s actually built in the US, came in far above estimates of this kind, so treat it as a design-basis cost rather than an achieved one.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 9 (2 x AP1000, 2,156 MW net, total capital cost $16.9bn).

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The estimate is presented as an overnight cost in 2023 dollars
rows.caveat: A 2023-dollar estimate for a six-module, 480 MW small modular reactor plant. No SMR of this design is operating in the United States, so unlike the gas and solar rows in this column there is no built example to check the estimate against.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 10 (6 x 80 MW SMR, 480 MW net).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: based on publicly available cost estimates for Vogtle units 3 and 4
rows.caveat: The low end reflects the cost attributed to Vogtle unit 4, the second of the pair, where industry estimates suggest roughly 30% was saved by building a repeat unit. It is one project in one state, not a class estimate, and assumes a 94% capacity factor over an 80-year life.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 footnote 4.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: based on publicly available cost estimates for Vogtle units 3 and 4
rows.caveat: The high end reflects the cost attributed to Vogtle unit 3, the first-of-a-kind unit, at a $12,300-$17,570/kW capital cost. A first US AP1000 in a generation is close to a worst case, and the figure is not comparable with the restart or SMR points on the same chart.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 footnote 4; high end of Lazard's capital cost range.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Estimate is highly illustrative and not directly comparable to other technologies presented herein
rows.caveat: Lazard's own words: an illustrative point for selected small modular reactor projects at different stages of development, built from disclosed capital estimates rather than from a completed plant. These projects expect to come online in 2030 or later, so the figure describes intentions, not costs anybody has paid.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 footnote 8; projects named are Clinch River, Darlington and Natrium.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Represents the illustrative LCOE of U.S. nuclear facilities which have announced restart
rows.caveat: An illustrative cost for restarting three shut reactors, including restart capital and decommissioning costs spread over a 20-year licence period. A restart reuses a site, a grid connection and a licence, so this number answers a different question from the new-build rows above it and should never be read as the cost of new nuclear.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 footnote 7; facilities named are Crane Clean Energy Center, Duane Arnold and Palisades.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Construction Time Months 84
rows.caveat: Construction time only, and an assumption rather than an observation: it excludes licensing, which for a US reactor is measured in years of its own. Vogtle units 3 and 4 took far longer than seven years from first concrete to commercial operation.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 assumptions page, U.S. Nuclear.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Reflects the marginal cost of operating fully depreciated gas, coal and nuclear facilities
rows.caveat: The going-forward cost of running an existing, fully depreciated coal plant at a 62% capacity factor on $1.90/MMBtu coal - fuel and operating costs only, with no capital recovery. Keeping a plant past its retirement date usually requires capital spending (environmental retrofits, turbine work) that this figure excludes entirely, as does any reliability-must-run payment.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 marginal cost page, Coal, low end.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Reflects the marginal cost of operating fully depreciated gas, coal and nuclear facilities
rows.caveat: The same measure at a 34% capacity factor and $2.95/MMBtu coal. Because fixed operating costs are spread over less output, a plant kept alive but run rarely costs roughly twice as much per MWh - which is the usual position of a unit whose retirement has been deferred for reliability.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 marginal cost page, Coal, high end.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.A (capacity factors, fossil-fuel generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for the whole US coal fleet, which rose from 42.6% in 2024 as load grew. It is a fleet-wide economic outcome; the specific units whose retirements get deferred are usually the older and less efficient ones, which run less than this. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Coal column.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Annual 2024, Table 8.1 Average Operating Heat Rate for Selected Energy Sources
rows.quote: Average Operating Heat Rate for Selected Energy Sources, 2014 through 2024
rows.caveat: The 2024 fleet-wide average operating heat rate for coal at utility and independent power producer plants, excluding combined heat and power and industrial plants. It is an as-run annual average including part-load operation, so it is not comparable with the new-build design heat rates quoted for gas elsewhere in this column.
rows.curator_notes: Coal column, 2024 row. The fleet average has drifted upward from 10,428 Btu/kWh in 2014.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The capital costs provided are overnight capital costs in 2023 price levels
rows.caveat: A 2023-dollar estimate for a 211 MW grid-connected simple-cycle plant of four aeroderivative turbines, including owner's costs and electrical interconnection. A behind-the-meter installation avoids the transmission interconnection but adds firm gas supply and site works, so this is not an on-site installed cost.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 3 (4 x 54 MW aeroderivative). The larger H-class frame machine, Case 4, is $836/kW.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: Lazard's gas peaking low case assumes the machine runs only 15% of the year, which is a peaker's duty cycle and the opposite of a data center's. Run the same turbine continuously and the capital component per MWh falls sharply, so this figure should not be read as the cost of on-site baseload generation.
rows.curator_notes: Components at the low end: $98 capital, $8 fixed O&M, $4 variable O&M, $35 fuel.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: higher capital costs, sustained interest rates, tariff pass-through and supply chain repricing
rows.caveat: The high case assumes a 10% capacity factor on a 250 MW plant. Almost the whole gap between this and the low case is the assumed running hours, not any difference in equipment, and neither case includes a capacity payment, which is how real peakers earn much of their revenue.
rows.curator_notes: Components at the high end: $213 capital, $19 fixed O&M, $5 variable O&M, $39 fuel.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.A (capacity factors, fossil-fuel generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for US grid-connected natural gas combustion turbines, which exist to cover peaks and therefore sit idle most of the year. On-site generation for a data center is intended to run continuously, so this fleet number describes a different job done by the same machine. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Natural Gas / Gas Turbine column. Gas internal combustion engines averaged 17.4%.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: Heat Rate, Higher Heating Value (HHV) Basis
rows.caveat: A design figure for a new four-unit aeroderivative simple-cycle plant on a higher-heating-value basis. Simple-cycle machines throw away the exhaust heat, which is why this is roughly 50% worse than the combined-cycle figure under path A1; it is not comparable with vendor lower-heating-value specifications.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 3. The H-class simple-cycle frame machine, Case 4, is 9,142 Btu/kWh.

rows.source_name: GE Vernova, 7HA Heavy Duty Gas Turbine factsheet
rows.quote: SC Net Heat Rate (Btu/kWh, LHV) 7884
rows.caveat: A turbine maker's simple-cycle specification for a 430 MW 7HA.03 at ISO conditions on a lower-heating-value basis. It is a large frame machine, not the packaged engine or aeroderivative skid most behind-the-meter projects install, and the lower-heating-value basis makes it look roughly a tenth better than EIA's higher-heating-value estimate above; the factsheet says its information is indicative.
rows.curator_notes: Factsheet SC PLANT PERFORMANCE row, 7HA.03 column.

rows.source_name: EIA, Cost and Performance Characteristics of New Generating Technologies, Annual Energy Outlook 2023
rows.quote: Overnight costs exclude interest accrued during plant construction and development
rows.caveat: EIA's modelling cost for a generic 10 MW fuel cell in 2022 dollars, including a 1.08 technological optimism factor applied to unproven designs. It is four years old and EIA's newer capital cost study does not cover fuel cells at all; it also excludes the gas supply and site work a data-center installation needs, so it is not comparable with a turbine's installed plant cost.
rows.curator_notes: AEO2023 Table 1. Base overnight cost before the optimism factor is $6,771/kW.

rows.source_name: EIA, Cost and Performance Characteristics of New Generating Technologies, Annual Energy Outlook 2023
rows.quote: Cost and performance characteristics of new central station electricity generating technologies
rows.caveat: A design assumption for a generic 10 MW fuel cell, implying roughly 53% efficiency - better than a simple-cycle turbine and close to a combined cycle. It is a modelling input rather than measured fleet performance, and fuel cell stacks lose efficiency over their life, which this does not capture.
rows.curator_notes: AEO2023 Table 1, Fuel cells row.

rows.source_name: Bloom Energy, company website
rows.quote: installed and operational in as little as 90 days
rows.caveat: A vendor's best case, quoted in days rather than the months used elsewhere in this column, and it measures installation - not the time from order, permit or gas service connection, which is what a buyer waits through. The claim sits on an undated marketing page carrying a 2026 copyright and is a target, not a delivered average.
rows.curator_notes: Homepage body text; publish_date is the day the page was opened because the page carries no date.

rows.source_name: EIA / Sargent & Lundy, Capital Cost and Performance Characteristics for Utility-Scale Power Generating Technologies (AEO2025)
rows.quote: The capital costs provided are overnight capital costs in 2023 price levels
rows.caveat: A 2023-dollar estimate for a 150 MW / 600 MWh lithium-ion system, which EIA also states as $436/kWh. A battery's cost scales with hours of storage, so a per-kW figure only means anything alongside its duration and is not comparable with a generator's per-kW cost. This is also a utility-scale grid installation, not a data-center backup or UPS package.
rows.curator_notes: Table 1-2, Case 19 (four-hour system).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Unsubsidized LCOS $/MWh $210 - $292
rows.caveat: A levelised cost of storage, not of energy: storage generates nothing, and this figure already includes $40/MWh to buy the power it later discharges. It assumes a 100 MW four-hour standalone system cycled 350 times a year, unsubsidised, so it cannot be compared with any generation row in this column.
rows.curator_notes: LCOS v11 key assumptions, utility-scale standalone four-hour, low case.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Unsubsidized LCOS $/MWh $210 - $292
rows.caveat: The high end of the same four-hour standalone case. Lazard reports storage costs rose this year, reversing earlier declines, which it attributes to tariffs on imported lithium-ion cells - so this figure is a snapshot of a moving tariff position rather than a settled cost.
rows.curator_notes: LCOS v11 key assumptions; two-hour systems run $215-$414/MWh.

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Reflects the marginal cost of operating fully depreciated gas, coal and nuclear facilities
rows.caveat: The going-forward cost of running an existing large reactor at a 94% capacity factor - fuel, operating costs and decommissioning accrual, with no capital recovery. This is the floor under what an owner would accept, not a contract price: the per-MWh prices in the large data-center nuclear agreements have not been disclosed.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 marginal cost page, U.S. Nuclear, low end (2,350 MW plant).

rows.source_name: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ Version 19.0
rows.quote: Reflects the marginal cost of operating fully depreciated gas, coal and nuclear facilities
rows.caveat: The same measure for a smaller 1,175 MW plant with higher fixed operating costs. Both ends describe the owner's cost, so the gap between roughly $30/MWh here and the prices reported around recent data-center nuclear deals is the owner's margin, not a cost of supply.
rows.curator_notes: LCOE v19 marginal cost page, U.S. Nuclear, high end.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.B (capacity factors, non-fossil generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for the whole US nuclear fleet, which is the physical availability a buyer is contracting for. It does not mean the data center runs on those electrons: a nuclear PPA is a financial claim on the plant's output while the site still draws from the grid. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Nuclear column.

rows.source_name: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Utility-Scale Solar, 2024 Edition (slides)
rows.quote: $35-$47/MWh for projects elsewhere in the continental United States
rows.caveat: A contract price, not a levelised cost: the bundled price of energy and renewable energy credits, levelised over a 20-25 year term in 2023 dollars, for solar PPAs signed in 2021 or later outside the West. It sits below an unsubsidised cost because the 30% investment tax credit is passed through by the seller, so it is not comparable with the Lazard rows in this column.
rows.curator_notes: Berkeley Lab Utility-Scale Solar 2024 Edition, slide 40; the West and CAISO band is $20-$30/MWh.

rows.source_name: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Utility-Scale Solar, 2024 Edition (slides)
rows.quote: $35-$47/MWh for projects elsewhere in the continental United States
rows.caveat: The top of the same band. These are contracts executed through 2024 and reported in 2023 dollars, so they predate the increase in offered renewable PPA prices through 2025 and 2026; a buyer signing today would not see these numbers.
rows.curator_notes: Berkeley Lab Utility-Scale Solar 2024 Edition, slide 40. The 2023 generation-weighted national average was $35/MWh on a sample of seven PPAs.

rows.source_name: EIA, Electric Power Monthly Table 6.07.B (capacity factors, non-fossil generators)
rows.quote: Capacity factors are a comparison of net generation with available capacity
rows.caveat: The 2025 average for the US wind fleet, given because most large corporate renewable PPAs are wind or solar and wind is the higher-output of the two. It is an annual average against summer capacity: the hours the output arrives do not line up with a constant data-center load, and the contract does not change that. EIA marks 2025 values preliminary.
rows.curator_notes: Annual row 2025, Wind column. Utility-scale solar photovoltaic averaged 24.4%.
